analysis.one_liner: Requires IRS audits and public reports of presidential tax returns and mandatory release by presidents and nominees.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 11 Senate cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a markup or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the IRS to promptly audit the president's tax returns and publish reports online showing what the audit found. It would also make presidential tax returns and audit files public, and require presidents and major-party presidential nominees to release three years of their tax returns. It covers the president's spouse and any businesses, trusts, or estates the president controls, so income can't simply be moved out of the personal return.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and the public. Today, whether a president is audited and what the audit finds is essentially invisible; the bill would put the president's returns, the audit's progress, and any proposed corrections online for anyone to see. Candidates would have to show their returns before election day, giving voters financial information they currently have no right to.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the IRS to examine each presidential income tax return as fast as practicable and publish an initial report within 90 days, updates every 180 days, and a final report describing each proposed adjustment and how it was resolved.

Carves a new exception to the confidentiality rules that normally keep tax returns secret, so the president's returns and the audit files (exam letters, adjustment proposals, appeals memos, closing documents) must be posted on the internet, with Social Security numbers, account numbers, addresses, and children's names redacted.

Requires sitting presidents and major-party presidential nominees to disclose their three most recent tax returns under the Ethics in Government Act, and makes it a penalty-triggering offense to falsify or willfully fail to file a required return; if they refuse, the Office of Government Ethics or the FEC can obtain the returns from the Treasury and post them anyway.

Defines the covered returns broadly to include a president's spouse and any corporation, partnership, trust, or estate the president or spouse controls (including entities moved to family members within the prior four years), so shifting income into a family business does not escape scrutiny.

analysis.who_pays: Presidents, their spouses, and their controlled businesses, trusts, and estates lose financial privacy and face mandatory, publicly reported audits. The IRS takes on new audit-reporting and publication work. That is the intended cost: the people who hold the most powerful office give up the tax secrecy every other taxpayer keeps.

drawbacks.text: The disclosure reaches beyond the president's personal return to the returns of controlled corporations, partnerships, trusts, and estates, putting family business finances on the internet with redaction limited to identification numbers, addresses, account numbers, minors, and employee names.

The IRS would have to publish reports while audits are still underway (an initial report within 90 days of filing, then updates every 180 days), meaning preliminary statements about unresolved examinations become public and the agency takes on a standing new reporting workload.
The requirement is narrow: it covers presidents and major-party presidential nominees only, not members of Congress, governors, or other officials whose tax secrecy remains unchanged.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but bounded: one officeholder's family loses tax privacy and the IRS gains reporting duties, with redaction rules to keep Social Security numbers and children out of public view. The benefit is a check on the most powerful person in government — the public currently has no way to know whether a president's returns are examined, what the examiners found, or whether proposed adjustments were quietly dropped. On balance the transparency gain outweighs the privacy loss, though the sweeping inclusion of controlled businesses and in-progress audit reports goes further than a minimal disclosure rule would.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it sat there until the two-year Congress ended without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden introduced the bill on April 25, 2023 with 10 Senate Democrats and 1 Senate independent as cosponsors.
The Senate's only action was to read it twice and refer it to the Committee on Finance; the action history shows nothing after that referral for the rest of the Congress.
The Finance Committee never held a markup or vote, the Senate never debated it, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting and future presidents, and presidential candidates who prefer not to release their tax returns, are better off — no law now requires disclosure, and the bill will have to be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Presidents and candidates who avoid tax disclosure

for.name: 10 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Sanders, Whitehouse, Cantwell, Warren, Van Hollen, Kaine, Welch, Klobuchar, Cardin, Markey).

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after it was referred on April 25, 2023.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote in the 20 months it existed.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Democrats or the independent Bernie Sanders, with no Republican support, but no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Presidents and their family business empires
industries.note: The bill's costs fall directly on whoever holds the presidency: mandatory audits with public progress reports, and online publication of personal returns plus the returns of controlled corporations, partnerships, trusts, and estates. That loss of privacy is the public's gain in oversight of the most powerful officeholder.

Nominees would have to file their three most recent tax returns with the FEC within 15 days of nomination, with the FEC authorized to obtain and publish returns they withhold. Voters would gain financial information about candidates that is currently voluntary to release.
